newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan dlr ends at 8-year low despite rate hike.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan dlr ends at 8-year low despite rate hike.

text.p: The Taiwan dollar sank anew to its lowest level since 1988 on Friday despite early speculative selling of greenbacks triggered by the central bank's decision to raise two key interest rates, dealers said.
The local unit, which fell dramatically all week, rebounded in early trade to as high as T$28.55, reacting to the central bank moves announced after the close of trade on Thursday.
But buying of the U.S. unit resumed in the afternoon, pulling the Taiwan dollar to close at T$28.752 -- its lowest close since October 1988.
Turnover through dealers was heavy at US$305 million.

"The central bank's decision to raise key interest rates and it's clear attempt to talk down speculation had some impact in the morning, but U.S. dollar buying is just too strong," said one dealer at a foreign bank.
Dealers said much of the greenback buying was in the form of non-delivery forward trading.

The central bank, saying it wanted to "stabilise the foreign exchange market", unveiled a modest tightening of monetary policy on Thursday, raising the rediscount rate to 5.25 percent from 5.00 and accommodations against secured loans to 5.625 percent from 5.375, effective from Friday.
Central bank governor Sheu Yuan-dong said the rate hikes were intended to maintain forex market stability, but dealers said the greenback's strength appeared to be unstoppable.
The U.S. dollar topped 119 yen for the first time in 11 weeks on Friday and was bobbing just below Monday's seven-and-a-half-year peak against the mark.
"If the U.S. dollar maintains its strength overseas, the Taiwan dollar will soon stand at above T$28.80 -- probably tomorrow," the dealer said of the half-day Saturday session.
Many local importers saw the central bank's rate hikes merely as a gesture with little substance, dealers said.
Some dealers said they detected mild intervention by the central bank shortly before the market close.

Sheu, speaking after his bank's quarterly board meeting, made clear the bank aimed to thwart the kind of speculative attacks that have shocked several southeast Asian currencies in July, though he noted that such attacks had not been conspicuous during Taiwan's steady currency depreciation.
"If there are abnormal factors intervening in the market, the central bank will adopt appropriate measures to maintain the foreign exchange market's stability," he said.
Sheu did not say what he meant by "appropriate measures".
Dealers said they expected the Taiwan dollar to trade in a T$28.70-90 range on Saturday -- raising the prospect of yet another eight-year low finish.
